newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton rates seen up in Pakistan, mixed in India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton rates seen up in Pakistan, mixed in India.

text.p: Cotton rates are likely to rise in Pakistan in the next week on shortage of quality cotton but will be mixed in India, dealers said on Friday.

Iqbal Usman, a dealer at the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA), said shortage of good quality cotton prompted a rise on Friday and new crop arrivals did not dampen prices because the quantity was small.

Pakistan aims to produce 10 million bales of cotton in 1997/98 (July-June) up from 8.783 million produced in 1996/97, short of the target of 10 million for the year due to bad weather, untimely rains and insect attack.
Pakistan Cotton Ginners Association has said 1996/97 cotton output reached 8.783 million bales by June 30, down from 9.938 million in the same period a year ago.

KCA's official spot rates for NIAB-78 1996/97 (July-June) crop rose 16.88 rupees to 2,351.88 per maund (37.32 kg) on Friday from Thursday.

On the kerb market, NIAB-78 was quoted at 2,325/2,340 rupees per maund, K-68 2,530/2,550 and MNH-93 2,540/2,550.
The KCA said Pakistan had shipped 125,515 bales by June 28 out of 164,756 booked for export by July 8, compared to 1.824 million and 2.328 million respectively in the year ago period.
In India, cotton prices were mixed in the week to Thursday as varieties from India's western state of Gujarat recovered while those from the northern state of Punjab fell, traders said.
Gujarat varieties firmed on reports of crop losses due to recent floods, they said. There was also speculative buying in the wake of the Indian cabinet's approval of futures trading in cotton.

"Cotton buying from yarn mills remained poor but speculative activity helped prices firm," a trader said. "The government has allowed forward trading in cotton...and traders are gearing up to start," he added.
"It will take some time to set up facilities required for forward trading in cotton as they involve a modern computer network," said Manubhai Amarsey, a leading trader.
In spot, Gujarat Kalyan rose 200 rupees to 14,000/14,200 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and wagad cotton 300 rupees to 13,000 per candy.
Long-staple Gujarat Sankar-4 gained 400/500 rupees to 17,000/18,000 rupees per candy for average variety and 19,500/20,500 for superior.
Punjab varieties remained subdued due to selling by traders triggered by satisfactory monsoon rains.
Punjab saw-ginned fell 10/25 rupees to 1,800/1,850 rupees per maund (37.32 kg). Bengal-deshi fell 10/30 rupees to 995/1,045 rupees per maund.
Traders said the progress of the four-month June-September monsoon had been satisfactory.
"Looking at the progress of the monsoon, sluggish mill buying, absence of a fresh export quota and unsold stock, I expect cotton prices to remain subdued in the coming days," Amarsey said.
($1 = 40.62 Pakistani rupees)
